title: Backend Composition
subject: main

axioms.text: Every entity has exactly one schema definition across slices and apps.
APIs come in two kinds: client (user-facing) and M2M (service-to-service).
Five layers, one responsibility each: middleware · router · service · repository · model.
The substrate is shared and transport-agnostic; only the edge changes.
sub: Service, repository and model never know how they were reached.
Each kind of caller — client, M2M, background — brings its own router and middlewares, and calls the same substrate.
A client — the API consumer — calls only the router.
The router calls its middlewares, then one service.
A middleware calls a repository for hydration reads only.
A service calls its own entity's repository, never another entity's.
Cross-entity calls are service to service; across backends, over the M2M edge.
Only a repository calls the database, through the model.
A repository carries no application logic; a model carries no logic.

axioms.text: Background works (cron jobs, agents, pipelines) plug into the service layer or run independently.

purpose.intro: Many callers reach the same slice operations — client requests, M2M calls, crons, agents. Layering puts the logic below the transport, in one substrate every caller passes through: the edge adapts the caller, the substrate holds the logic. Adding a caller or a datastore means writing an edge, not reimplementing the core. And because every slice's API has the same five layers and the same strict chain, a developer knows where anything lives before opening a folder.

reference.statement: The substrate — service, repository, model, AC engine — is reached from different edges. What differs per caller is middleware and router; the substrate is shared.

claims.text: Client-facing and machine-to-machine routes are distinct top-level paths: `/api/client/*` for end-user agents, `/api/m2m/*` for server-to-server.
An external provider that ships its own router mounts under those two namespaces — `api/client/<provider>/*` — never alongside them, so `client/*` covers every endpoint a client hits.
Auth endpoints are their own request class: `/api/client/auth/*` is provider-owned, session lifecycle only, and access-context hydration never runs on it.
Backends with no API surface (e.g. cron over self-contained libraries) are exempt from the 5-layer/2-path rule.
Process singletons — the server, the db pool, the redis connection — are created once, in top-level files at the app's `src/` root: one file, one instantiation.

claims.text: Five layers, one responsibility each: middleware (hydration/auth) → router (HTTP transport) → service (business logic) → repository (data access) → model.
Only repositories touch the database — read and write, no exception. Two valid paths: middleware→router→service→repo→db, or middleware→repo→db (hydration reads only).
One abstraction per file, maximally separated.

imagesAndDiagrams.title: What each layer owns — and what it must never do
The data path — any other layer calling the DB is a violation

claims.text: Middleware hydrates blindly — no business branching (no if/else on session validity; the service throws when there's no session). Hydration is the one sanctioned exception to "all DB access goes through AC": it must read the DB *before* AC exists (it produces the bag AC needs), so it uses a dedicated method minted by scoped AC that reaches the DB without a Scope. Kept safe by being a public service method with no route exposing it.
Protected requests pass a fixed linear middleware sequence before the handler: set/validate session → fetch roles/memberships → hydrate effective-permissions bag → unmet-requirements gate.
Routers are thin: extract request identity, zod-parse input, call one service, return. Never import a repo or db; zero business logic; never decide access.
Design and finalize routes first — the route is the interface; the service shape emerges from routes + repo.
The service owns the business logic: the conditionals, the decisions, the validations — and the throws. Only a service throws, and only typed `AppError` subclasses, never a raw `new Error()`.

A Helper is self-sufficient: no db access, data passed in. A helper consumed by one service stays with that service. A helper consumed by more than one goes to the nearest `shared/` level above all its consumers — the same sharing principle as everywhere.
One repository = one table. Every model/table gets a repository and a service — the service may be a thin route→repo proxy.

The standard repo shape: `findAll` (paginated, identical WHERE for list + count, returns `{ rows, total }`) · `findByIds` (always an array — want one? pass `[id]`; no `findById`) · `create` · `update` · `delete`.

Extra repo methods only for a genuinely specific query shape, with a stated reason. Named for the field filtered, plural, array params: `findAllByOrgIds`, never `listFor*`. Specificity and product constraints are the role of services, not repos.

Repos are dumb: zero business logic — no conditional, switch, throw, or decision. A repo never throws; it returns empty state. A permission-style lookup returns rows/count, never a boolean (boolean = business logic = service).

A repository never joins. The moment a repo joins a second entity, that entity's rows enter the query with its access control missing — that is the reason. A cross-entity read is a DB view or service enrichment: the service gets its own rows, asks the other entity's service for what is missing, joins, and serves.

A view ends in `View`, and its owner follows its rows. If the served rows are entity A's rows — however enriched — the view lives in A's repository as a queryable relation. If the served rows are an abstraction that is no single entity, the view gets a repository of its own.

reference.statement: One hand-written shape per entity — the model. Everything below it is inferred or derived, so the compiler chains every schema and type back to the model and nothing drifts silently.

claims.text: One canonical **model** per entity, one declarer — re-declaring elsewhere is a violation. Models carry no business logic.
Models: `<entity>.model.ts` + `<entity>.schemas.ts` side by side, in a folder named `models` (never `schemas`).

The model is the only hand-written entity shape. Entity zod schemas are inferred from it (`createSelectSchema` / `createInsertSchema`); types exist only through `z.infer`. A hand-written entity schema or a hand-written interface duplicating one is a violation.

An input schema is a derivation: `entitySchema.pick/omit/extend` plus refinements. The diff is the only hand-authored part — it is the business decision of what a caller may set. A from-scratch `z.object` over entity fields is a violation.

A composed shape — a wire view, an app-specific type — takes its entity fields from the inferred schemas (`Schema.shape.field`) and declares only what is genuinely new (computed fields). The service composing it returns `satisfies` the composed type, so drifting from the model is a compile error.
Wire schemas are the client contract and live in the slice's `shared/`; web infers its types from them — never from entity schemas, so the persistence shape never leaks to a client.

Module entities in `<seed slice>/api/models/`; product slice entities in `apps/main/slices/product/<f>/api/models/` — same shape, one declarer each; `src/models/index.ts` re-exports only (db-client aggregation), declares nothing.
Immutable classification fields (e.g. org type) never change post-creation; denormalize them onto dependent records for convenience.
Request-scoped, client-owned state (e.g. active org) is never persisted — the client sends it every request; the server re-derives and re-checks. (Exception: real-time server-initiated actions.)

claims.text: Repos use `find*`; services use `get*`; `load*` is reserved for config — and a config loader is never named like a DB accessor. Layers don't share one name: repo `findByX` → service `getByX`.
`getMy*` is allowed in services.
Multi-record lookups are plural and take array params; singular names only for single-unique-entity lookups.
Mutate endpoints are named `update`, not `patch`.
Recovery/reset endpoints are named after the slice object (`completePasswordRecovery`), not generic verbs.
Public endpoint names never leak internal mechanism (`register`, not `flows`); services are named for what they do, not how (`auth`, not `relay`).
`getCurrent*` is `getLatest*` when no rollback exists — names reflect what the system actually does.

`me` namespace = data of the requesting user and no organization. A route is `me` only if both hold: it touches no other user's data, and it works without an active org. Fails the first → `admin` or the entity's route; fails the second → the entity's route under the active org. `me` routes are exactly the ones allowed to run with no active-org context.
Route grouping follows the primary entity retrieved, not URL nesting (`/organization/invitations` is an invitation route); a route path need not match its service name.
Identity-provider-specific lookups never live in the generic user model/service — they belong to the integration layer.
A [[lifecycle hook|hook]] carries the bare fact only — message/template content is exported separately.
A seed slice that receives an external webhook owns it exclusively and translates it into an internal lifecycle hook; other seed slices react to the hook, never the webhook.

reference.statement: An external provider is a system a seed slice collaborates with that owns its own persistence. Providers do not appear in the five-layer model: their internal writes are theirs, and the seed slice's responsibility ends at the adapter call.

claims.text: Every touch-point with an external provider routes through ONE abstraction/integration layer in its owning seed slice. App code never calls provider endpoints or imports the provider directly — the app must not even know the provider's name.

Providers are called from the **service** layer, optionally through a seed slice-owned **adapter** — a thin facade that translates between our slice and the provider's API. Adapters carry no business logic.

A provider's internal storage is not our database, even when co-deployed — provider calls do not violate "only repositories access our database". Mirroring provider state into our db goes through a repository like any other write; the adapter or service sequences the provider call and the mirror write.
Integration code for a **consumed** provider lives in its own folder, not `api/` — `api/` is what you expose, not what you consume.

claims.text: Every endpoint returning a collection follows one standard contract via the `list-query` lib — no carve-outs. Query params: `page` · `pageSize` · `sort` (whitelisted per endpoint, mandatory default stable sort, unknown field → 400) · `search` (only on endpoints declaring themselves searchable, unsupported → 400, never silent-ignore). Response: `{ rows, total }`.

Always paginated, defaults always apply. `total` reflects the full scoped count — same WHERE as the list query, never diverging. Past-end returns `{ rows: [], total }`, never 404. A stable tiebreaker column is appended as the final sort field — pagination without one is forbidden.
